summary: No state body sites wind or solar in Alabama; local governments decide. Local acts give Baldwin County zoning power over wind facilities and require a local permit for any commercial wind system in Cherokee, DeKalb and Etowah counties; a utility building a plant also needs a certificate of convenience and necessity from the Public Service Commission.
amendments_note: History notes on alison.legislature.state.al.us as of 2026-10-09: 45-2-262 Act 2013-440; 45-10-260.02 Act 2014-190; 45-25-260.02 Acts 2015-348 and 2015-387; 45-28-260.02 Act 2014-191; 37-4-28 Code 1940; no later amendment shown. 2026 bills for a one-year statewide solar moratorium (HB617, SB354, SB372), county solar zoning (HB618, SB358) and solar permits and decommissioning (HB623) show no act number on the legislature site, so none was enacted.

summary: Statewide, a wind energy facility may not encroach on or adversely affect military operations and readiness, and a local government may not approve one until the developer shows a Department of Defense Siting Clearinghouse finding of no presumed risk, a mitigation agreement, or an FAA determination of no hazard (or the approval is conditioned on one); notice to the Clearinghouse is due at least 270 days before construction.
amendments_note: 11-106-6 history: Act 2021-114 s2; Act 2025-139 s1. Act 2025-139 (2025 SB 91) amended 11-106-3, -4 and -6 to require local approval for tall structures within 2 miles of a military installation and drop a minimum acreage from the definition of military installation; the wind provisions read here are the current text.

summary: To get a state permit, each turbine must sit at least the greater of 3.5 times its tip height or 2,500 feet from a nonparticipating property line (waivable to 1.1 times height) and one mile from schools, hospitals, nursing homes, churches, city or town limits, state or federal parks and public airports; noise may not exceed 35 dBA at a nonparticipating dwelling or 45 dBA at the property line, and shadow flicker is capped at 30 hours a year. Local wind rules may be stricter but not less restrictive.
amendments_note: New in 2025 (Act 945, approved 2025-04-21), after the June 2024 inventory. A web search found no later amendment as of 2026-10-09; the codified text on Lexis was not read.

summary: Counties, cities and towns decide siting of wind and solar photovoltaic projects through zoning. The state Power Plant and Transmission Line Siting Committee issues certificates of environmental compatibility only for thermal, nuclear or hydroelectric units of 100 MW or more, a definition that names no wind or photovoltaic technology; where a certificate is needed, the committee may override a local rule it finds unreasonably restrictive.
amendments_note: azleg.gov section pages show no history notes. The 2025 and 2026 bills that would have added county rules for wind and solar (2025 SB 1150 House engrossed version; 2026 HB 2337 and HB 2338, which would have added 11-820.05) show no chapter number in the azleg.gov bill API as of 2026-10-09, and 11-820.05 on azleg.gov is an unrelated assisted living section. The similar 2023 HB 2618 was vetoed.

summary: Counties and cities decide most wind, solar and storage projects, but a developer of a photovoltaic or terrestrial wind plant of 50 MW or more, or a storage system of 200 MWh or more, may instead apply (until June 30, 2030) to the California Energy Commission, which then has exclusive power to certify the site. Thermal plants of 50 MW or more, including solar thermal, must be certified by the Commission; wind and photovoltaic plants are excluded from that mandatory track.
amendments_note: Section histories on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov as of 2026-10-09: 25545 amended by Stats. 2025, ch. 372 (AB 531), eff. 2026-01-01 (adds geothermal and other facility types); 25545.1 and 25545.2 amended by Stats. 2025, ch. 119 (SB 254), eff. 2025-09-19 (25545.1 now sets an application deadline of June 30, 2030); 25500 last amended 1976; 25120 last amended 1988. Per secondary sources, 2025 SB 283 (signed 2025-10-06, eff. 2026-01-01) applies NFPA 855 fire standards to storage certified under the opt-in program; not read. 2025 AB 303 (3,200-foot storage setback) did not pass.

summary: When a developer of an eligible wind, photovoltaic or storage project uses the Energy Commission opt-in process, the Commission certificate replaces local permits and supersedes local ordinances, including those of charter cities; the Coastal Commission, State Lands Commission and water boards keep their authority.
amendments_note: Amended by Stats. 2025, ch. 119 (SB 254), eff. 2025-09-19, per the section history on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov as of 2026-10-09; the supersession language in (b)(1) and the charter city clause in (c) are in the current text.

summary: Counties and municipalities decide siting of wind, solar and storage through their land use codes; the state gives them technical help and model codes but has no siting permit of its own. A public utility also needs a certificate of public convenience and necessity from the Public Utilities Commission, which by statute does not decide siting, and its new plants must comply with local zoning unless it wins an appeal under 29-20-108.
amendments_note: Source notes in Colorado Revised Statutes 2024 (official uncertified printout on content.leg.colorado.gov): 40-5-101 last amended L. 2012 (HB 12-1312); 29-20-401 to -405 added L. 2024 (SB 24-212), eff. 2024-05-21. The 2025 edition PDF returned HTTP 404 on 2026-10-09, so 2025 and 2026 changes were checked only by web search, which found no later amendment.

summary: For generating facilities proposed by a public utility or power authority, the local government must act within 90 days of a final application (120 days of a preliminary one) or the application is deemed approved, and the utility may appeal a denial or unreasonable conditions to the Public Utilities Commission, which balances local and statewide interests. Independent developers that are not utilities do not get this appeal.
amendments_note: 29-20-108 source note (CRS 2024): added L. 2000; (2),(4),(5) L. 2001; (2) amended L. 2005 and L. 2014 (HB 14-1129); (3) amended and (6) added L. 2022 (HB 22-1104); (7) added L. 2023 (SB 23-016). No 2025 or 2026 amendment found by web search; the 2025 edition was not available to check.

summary: For facilities under its jurisdiction the Siting Council decides location and type, gives municipal regulations only the weight it deems appropriate, and its certificate replaces state and municipal approvals on public need. Town zoning commissions and inland wetland agencies may issue orders restricting a proposed generating facility within 65 days of the application, but the Council may affirm, modify or revoke those orders by a vote of six members.
amendments_note: 16-50x history note on cga.ct.gov (revised to 2025-01-01) ends with P.A. 07-222; not in the 2026 Supplement list of amended sections; no 2026 amendment found by web search.

summary: Siting Council rules require wind turbines to be set back from all property lines at least 2.5 times turbine height for projects over 65 MW (certificate) or 1.5 times height for smaller projects (declaratory ruling), or the manufacturer distance if greater; setbacks may be waived by neighbor consent or a two-thirds Council vote but never below 1.5 times height from an occupied home. Shadow flicker is capped at 30 hours a year at any occupied structure, and noise must meet state noise control rules.
statute_citation: Conn. Agencies Regs. 16-50j-95(a)-(c); see also 16-50j-92 to 16-50j-94
amendments_note: Regulation shows Effective May 9, 2014 on eregulations.ct.gov as of 2026-10-09; no later amendment shown.
source: Conn. Agencies Regs. 16-50j-95(a)-(c); see also 16-50j-92 to 16-50j-94

summary: A solar photovoltaic facility of 2 MW or more on prime farmland or forestland may be approved by declaratory ruling only if the Department of Agriculture states in writing that it will not materially affect the land as prime farmland, or the Department of Energy and Environmental Protection states that it will not materially affect the land as core forest, and the applicant posts a bond for decommissioning and restoring the farmland soils.
amendments_note: Added by P.A. 17-218, eff. 2017-07-01; bond added by P.A. 23-163, eff. 2023-06-29; bond extended to declaratory rulings by P.A. 25-127, eff. 2025-07-08 (2026 Supplement history note on cga.ct.gov). No 2026 amendment found by web search.

summary: Counties and municipalities decide siting of wind and solar; state land use review by the Office of State Planning Coordination is advisory and the local jurisdiction keeps final decision-making authority. A separate statute bars local rules stricter than set limits only for residential wind systems, not utility-scale projects.
amendments_note: Section credits on delcode.delaware.gov as of 2026-10-09: 9206 shows 74 Del. Laws c. 186 only; 8060 shows 77 Del. Laws c. 147 and c. 329. A web search found no 2024 to 2026 Delaware statute setting state siting rules for utility-scale wind, solar or storage; 2025 HB 269 and SB 210 concern grid interconnection, not siting (news reports, bills not read).

state_body: Florida Siting Board (with the Department of Environmental Protection Siting Coordination Office)
summary: A steam or solar electrical power plant of 75 MW or more must be certified by the state under the Power Plant Siting Act, and a smaller one may opt in; certification replaces local permits. Below 75 MW, solar is decided by local governments, which must treat it as a permitted use in agricultural zoning. No statute gives the state a siting role for wind, which is banned near the coast and offshore.
amendments_note: History notes in the 2026 Florida Statutes on flsenate.gov as of 2026-10-09: 403.506 last amended ch. 2008-227; 403.503 amended by s. 7, ch. 2024-186 (CS/HB 1645, eff. 2024-07-01), which added a definition of gross capacity measuring a solar facility in alternating current at the point before interconnection; the 75 MW threshold in (14) is unchanged; 403.510 last amended ch. 90-331.

summary: For a certified power plant (solar of 75 MW or more, or a smaller one whose applicant opts in), the state preempts regulation and certification of the site, and any conflicting local ordinance or rule is superseded.
amendments_note: 403.510 history: s. 1, ch. 73-33; s. 9, ch. 76-76; s. 14, ch. 90-331; no later amendment in the 2026 edition on flsenate.gov.

summary: A photovoltaic solar facility must be a permitted use in every agricultural land use category and agricultural zoning district in unincorporated areas, subject only to the setbacks and landscaped buffers that apply to similar agricultural uses; county buffer and landscaping rules for solar may not exceed those for comparable permitted uses. Since 2026 solar builders must also follow added stormwater and erosion control practices.
amendments_note: Amended by s. 2, ch. 2026-2, which added subsection (5) on construction best management practices (erosion and sediment control plans, 100-year 24-hour storm design, certified inspectors; Northwest Florida rule applies to applications filed after 2026-07-01); compared the 2025 and 2026 editions on flsenate.gov. Subsections (3) and (4) unchanged since ch. 2021-178.

summary: Florida bans building or expanding any offshore wind energy facility, any wind turbine or wind facility within 1 mile of the coastline or of the Atlantic or Gulf Intracoastal Waterway, and any wind turbine on state waters or submerged lands; turbines installed before July 1, 2024 may keep operating. Turbines covered are those able to produce more than 10 kW.
amendments_note: Created by s. 12, ch. 2024-186 (CS/HB 1645), eff. 2024-07-01 (sec. 23 of the session law on laws.flrules.org); history note in the 2026 edition on flsenate.gov shows no later amendment as of 2026-10-09.

summary: Counties decide siting of wind and solar through zoning and county planning commission special permits; there is no state siting board. The state Land Use Commission must also approve a special permit for land over 15 acres in the agricultural district.
amendments_note: HRS 205-6 history shows am. L 2025, c 236, s17 (Act 236, a biosecurity act that renames agencies; not a siting change). No other change after 2021 shown on data.capitol.hawaii.gov as of 2026-10-09.

summary: Solar facilities may not be built on agricultural-district land with the best (class A) soils, and on class B or C soils they are limited to 10 percent of the parcel or 20 acres, whichever is less, unless a county special permit is granted (with Land Use Commission approval over 15 acres) and the area is offered for farming at reduced rent and bonded for decommissioning. Wind facilities are a permitted use in the agricultural district if compatible with agriculture.
amendments_note: HRS 205-4.5 history shows am. L 2024, c 182 (overnight camps) and am. L 2025, c 255 (landfill siting); HRS 205-2 history shows am. L 2025, c 255. I read both session laws (SLH2024_Act182.pdf, SLH2025_Act255.pdf on data.capitol.hawaii.gov): neither changes the solar or wind provisions.

summary: Cities and counties decide siting of wind and solar through planning and zoning. A public utility (electrical corporation) building a plant also needs a certificate from the Idaho Public Utilities Commission, and a local order that conflicts with a specific PUC order is void to the extent of the conflict, but no state body sites merchant wind or solar.
amendments_note: 67-6528 history: added 1975, no later amendment shown; 61-526 history: last am. 1970; both on legislature.idaho.gov as of 2026-10-09. 2025 H 146 (wind lighting) added 21-515B, see ID-other-1. Web searches found no 2025 or 2026 Idaho siting statute for wind or solar (2025 H 317 and H 387 died).

state_body: Idaho Transportation Department, Division of Aeronautics
summary: A new wind energy conversion system (5 or more turbines at least 50 feet tall) may not begin commercial operation after July 1, 2025 unless the owner applies to the FAA for aircraft-detection or other light-mitigating technology, and must install it within 24 months of approval; existing systems must apply from January 1, 2026 and install within 60 months of approval.
statute_citation: Idaho Code 21-515B (2025 Idaho Sess. Laws ch. 153, H 146)
amendments_note: Added 2025, ch. 153, sec. 1 (H 146, emergency clause, effective 2025-03-24); no later amendment shown on legislature.idaho.gov as of 2026-10-09.
source: Idaho Code 21-515B (2025 Idaho Sess. Laws ch. 153, H 146)

summary: Counties grant siting approval or special use permits for commercial wind, solar and (from 2026-06-01) energy storage facilities under state-set limits; the state has no permitting authority of its own. Since 2026-06-01 the Illinois Commerce Commission may issue a siting certificate for a facility of 50 MW or more in unincorporated areas if a local government denies or fails to act in violation of the state siting law (see IL-local_preemption-3).

Counties may adopt standards for commercial wind and solar facilities but none more restrictive than the statute, may not ban them (even temporarily) in agricultural or industrial districts, must approve compliant applications, and may not set stricter sound, height, decommissioning or property-value conditions. The law exempts projects filed before 2023-01-27, an industrial enterprise zone near the I-88/I-39 interchange (Lee-Ogle, added by P.A. 103-81) and an area in Madison County (added by P.A. 104-458).
amendments_note: Amended by P.A. 103-81 (SB 1127, eff. 2023-06-09: Lee-Ogle enterprise zone carve-out in (u)), 103-580 (eff. 2023-12-08, not read), 104-417 (revisory), 104-458 (eff. 2026-06-01: Madison County carve-out in (u)(4)), 104-480 (eff. 2026-07-01). Current text read on ilga.gov 2026-10-09.

summary: From 2026-06-01, counties with zoning may regulate stand-alone energy storage systems only within limits set by statute: no requirements stricter than the statute or NFPA 855, no stricter sound limits than the Pollution Control Board rules, and compliant applications must be approved.
amendments_note: New section added by P.A. 104-458 (SB 25, eff. 2026-06-01); also amended by P.A. 104-480 (eff. 2026-07-01). Postdates the inventory.

summary: A developer of a wind, solar or storage facility of 50 MW or more in an unincorporated area may petition the Illinois Commerce Commission when a local government violates the state siting law; the Commission may issue a siting certificate if the local government denied the project, missed the statutory deadline, or never adopted a compliant ordinance, and the certificate authorizes construction.
amendments_note: New Article XXIII added by P.A. 104-458 (eff. 2026-06-01); 23-115 also amended by P.A. 104-477 (eff. 2026-06-26), which added the missed-deadline and no-compliant-ordinance grounds. Postdates the inventory.

summary: Statute sets the maximum setbacks a county may require: for wind towers 2.1 times blade-tip height from nonparticipating homes and community buildings and 1.1 times from nonparticipating property lines and roads, plus a 30-hour yearly shadow-flicker limit; for solar 150 feet from nonparticipating homes and 50 feet from property lines and roads, fencing of 6 to 25 feet, and panels no taller than 20 feet. Sound limits may be no stricter than state Pollution Control Board rules.
amendments_note: Same amendment history as IL-local_preemption-1; subsection (e) setbacks unchanged in the current text read 2026-10-09.

summary: Counties regulating stand-alone energy storage must require setbacks of 150 feet from occupied community buildings and nonparticipating homes, 50 feet from their property lines and from road rights-of-way, and perimeter fencing of 7 to 25 feet; nonparticipating owners may waive the setbacks.
amendments_note: New section added by P.A. 104-458 (eff. 2026-06-01); amended by P.A. 104-480 (eff. 2026-07-01).

summary: Counties and municipalities decide siting of wind and solar through local zoning; there is no state siting permit. State default standards apply only in communities that volunteer to become wind or solar energy ready communities (see IN-state_setback_standard-1 and -2).
amendments_note: Not checked on the official site (see note). News reports say 2025 SEA 425 (energy production zones) excludes wind and solar from its zoning bypass; I did not read SEA 425.

summary: In a county or municipality that voluntarily adopts the state wind standards, turbines must be set back 3 times tip height from nonparticipating homes, 1.1 times from nonparticipating property lines, roads and airport runways, 1 mile from state parks and municipal boundaries (waivable by the municipality), and meet a 50 dBA hourly sound limit at homes; local height limits may be no stricter than FAA rules.
amendments_note: Could not check for amendments after the 2022 printing on iga.in.gov (see note). Web searches found no 2025 or 2026 act amending IC 8-1-41.

summary: In a county or municipality that voluntarily adopts the state solar standards, commercial solar must be set back 250 feet from nonparticipating homes (or less with a landscape buffer), 50 feet from nonparticipating property lines and 10 to 40 feet from roads, panels may be no taller than 25 feet at full tilt, and sound may not exceed a 50 dBA hourly average at neighboring homes.
amendments_note: Could not check for amendments after the 2022 printing on iga.in.gov (see note). Web searches found no 2025 or 2026 act amending IC 8-1-42.

summary: Cities and counties decide siting of wind and solar through planning and zoning; a merchant generator built after 2001 that is not in a regulated rate base may opt out of Kansas Corporation Commission jurisdiction, so no state body sites these projects.
amendments_note: 12-741 history: L. 1991 only. 66-104 history ends L. 2024, ch. 69 (solar eminent domain, see KS-other-1). As shown on ksrevisor.gov 2026-10-09. 2025 SB 233 (county decommissioning agreements) appears to have stalled in committee (search result only).

summary: For eminent domain purposes, siting wind turbines or solar generating equipment is not a public utility activity, so neither utilities nor developers may condemn land for these facilities.
amendments_note: Solar was added by L. 2024, ch. 69 (2024 SB 455, conference report carrying SB 457, approved 2024-04-22, eff. July 1); the wind clause predates it (the revisor memo on SB 457 calls it existing law). History line on ksrevisor.gov, 2026-10-09.

state_body: Kentucky State Board on Electric Generation and Transmission Siting
summary: A merchant generating facility of 10 MW or more that sells at wholesale needs a construction certificate from the state siting board, and local ordinances, permits and planning and zoning setbacks still apply and prevail over a conflicting board order. Smaller facilities are left to local government.
amendments_note: 278.704 and 278.718 amended by 2026 Ky. Acts ch. 152 (HB 677, became law without signature 2026-04-14, eff. 2026-07-15), and 278.704 also by ch. 198 (HB 869). 278.700 last amended 2014. Per KRS history notes on apps.legislature.ky.gov, 2026-10-09.

state_body: Kentucky State Board on Electric Generation and Transmission Siting
summary: A siting board certificate may not issue unless any wind turbine is at least 1,000 feet from adjoining property lines and all generating structures are 2,000 feet from any residential neighborhood, school, hospital or nursing home; since 2026-07-15 wind turbine hub height is capped at 350 feet. Local planning and zoning limits take precedence where adopted, and the board may grant deviations from the state distances.
amendments_note: Amended by 2026 Ky. Acts ch. 152, s25 (HB 677, eff. 2026-07-15): added the 350-foot hub height limit and decommissioning bond carve-out; also 2026 ch. 198, s56 (HB 869), codified together. Earlier: 2023 Ky. Acts ch. 140 and 2014 Ky. Acts ch. 88 (HB 291, the source Sabin cites).

state_body: Kentucky State Board on Electric Generation and Transmission Siting
summary: Since 2026-07-15 an applicant for a wind facility certificate must certify that turbines will not be artificially lit except as required by law and that shadow flicker will be minimized and will not significantly harm neighboring uses, and the board considers compliance when deciding.
amendments_note: Added by 2026 Ky. Acts ch. 152, ss26-27 (HB 677, eff. 2026-07-15); 278.706 also amended by ch. 198, s57. Postdates the inventory.

state_body: Louisiana Department of Conservation and Energy
summary: Parish and municipal zoning governs siting, and the state Department of Conservation and Energy must also permit solar facilities of 10 acres or more (decommissioning and bonding), solar facilities of 75 acres or more (siting standards), every onshore wind project and renewable energy batteries (rules due by 2026-08-31).
amendments_note: 30:1131, 30:1141 to 30:1145 enacted by 2025 La. Acts No. 279 (HB 459, eff. 2025-08-01). 30:1154 last amended by 2023 Acts No. 150 and No. 455. The department was renamed from Energy and Natural Resources to Conservation and Energy. No 2026 act shown in the history notes on legis.la.gov as of 2026-10-09.

state_body: Louisiana Department of Conservation and Energy
summary: Solar facilities of 75 acres or more outside industrial-zoned or certified sites, begun after 2026-01-01, must keep 300 feet from residential property lines (with a 35 to 50 foot vegetative barrier) unless the owner agrees otherwise, 100 feet from water bodies and 50 feet from roads, and may not raise noise more than 10 dBA above ambient at the property line. A parish with its own solar ordinance may opt out of these standards by resolution.
amendments_note: Enacted by 2025 La. Acts No. 279 (HB 459, eff. 2025-08-01); no later amendment shown on legis.la.gov as of 2026-10-09. Postdates the inventory.

summary: The Energy Facilities Siting Board issues a single consolidated permit for solar and wind facilities of 25 MW or more (solar measured in DC) and storage of 100 MWh or more; smaller clean energy facilities are permitted by the city or town under uniform state standards, with a 12-month deadline and de novo review by the siting division director.
statute_citation: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, sections 69G and 69T; ch. 25A, section 21 (as added or amended by St. 2024, c. 239)
amendments_note: Changed after the inventory: St. 2024, c. 239 (signed Nov. 2024) section 74 added ch. 164 sections 69T to 69W, effective March 1, 2026 (c. 239 section 139), and section 23 added ch. 25A section 21. Section 132 says EFSB regulations apply to projects submitted on and after July 1, 2026. Section 69G now defines "generating facility" and "large clean energy generation facility" at 25 MW, replacing the 100 MW threshold the inventory describes. No later amendment shown in the section notes on malegislature.gov as of 2026-10-09.
source: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, sections 69G and 69T; ch. 25A, section 21 (as added or amended by St. 2024, c. 239)

summary: No local zoning ordinance or bylaw may prohibit or unreasonably regulate solar energy systems except where necessary to protect public health, safety or welfare.
amendments_note: St. 2024, c. 239 section 37 replaced "department of public utilities" with "energy facilities siting board" in the public service corporation zoning exemption paragraphs of section 3; the solar sentence itself is unchanged in the text shown on malegislature.gov as of 2026-10-09.

summary: For large clean energy facilities, the siting board consolidated permit stands in for all municipal, regional and state permits, and is deemed granted if the board misses its deadline; for small facilities, local governments must apply uniform state standards and a missed 12-month deadline produces a constructive approval.
statute_citation: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, sections 69G and 69T(i); ch. 25A, section 21(b), (d) to (g)
amendments_note: New law after the inventory: St. 2024, c. 239 section 74 (69T, effective March 1, 2026) and section 23 (25A section 21). None later shown on malegislature.gov as of 2026-10-09.
source: Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 164, sections 69G and 69T(i); ch. 25A, section 21(b), (d) to (g)

summary: Grid-connected generating stations need a certificate of public convenience and necessity (or an exemption or distributed generation certificate) from the Public Service Commission, and front-of-meter storage needs Commission approval; for wholesale or community solar of 1 to 2 MW the local jurisdiction checks the state siting standards instead. Counties still issue local permits but may not require conditional use or special exception approval.
amendments_note: Enacted by 2025 Md. Laws ch. 623 (SB 931, Renewable Energy Certainty Act, eff. 2025-07-01; HB 1036 is ch. 624). 2026 bills to change it (HB 460 lowering the priority preservation cap to 2 percent, SB 683, SB 265) show no action after committee hearings on mgaleg.maryland.gov as of 2026-10-09. 7-207 also carries a contingency note for 2025 ch. 572 (two versions shown).

summary: Local governments may not adopt zoning that prohibits solar generating stations (over 1 MW, wholesale or community solar) or deny site plans that meet the state siting standards, must expedite review, and must treat projects of 5 MW or less as a permitted use, subject to the growth-area and priority preservation exceptions in MD-other-1.
amendments_note: Enacted by 2025 Md. Laws ch. 623 (SB 931, Renewable Energy Certainty Act, eff. 2025-07-01; HB 1036 is ch. 624). 2026 bills to change it (HB 460 lowering the priority preservation cap to 2 percent, SB 683, SB 265) show no action after committee hearings on mgaleg.maryland.gov as of 2026-10-09.

summary: Local governments may not adopt zoning that prohibits front-of-the-meter energy storage or deny site plans that meet the state requirements, and must expedite review and adopt standard review processes.
amendments_note: Enacted by 2025 Md. Laws ch. 623 (SB 931, Renewable Energy Certainty Act, eff. 2025-07-01; HB 1036 is ch. 624). 2026 bills to change it (HB 460 lowering the priority preservation cap to 2 percent, SB 683, SB 265) show no action after committee hearings on mgaleg.maryland.gov as of 2026-10-09.

summary: Solar generating stations over 1 MW (other than agrivoltaics) must keep 150 feet from homes and 100 feet from property lines, keep fencing at most 20 feet tall and 50 feet from roads, provide a vegetative buffer up to 35 feet wide, emit no visible light at night, and average no more than 15 feet in height; a county siting agreement may set looser terms.
amendments_note: Enacted by 2025 Md. Laws ch. 623 (SB 931, Renewable Energy Certainty Act, eff. 2025-07-01; HB 1036 is ch. 624). 2026 bills to change it (HB 460 lowering the priority preservation cap to 2 percent, SB 683, SB 265) show no action after committee hearings on mgaleg.maryland.gov as of 2026-10-09.

summary: Ground-mounted solar over 5 MW may not be sited on land that on 2025-01-01 was in a Tier 1 or Tier 2 growth area, a medium or high density residential area, or a mixed-use area with homes, and solar in a priority preservation area established before 2025 is capped at 5 percent of that area's acreage.
amendments_note: Enacted by 2025 Md. Laws ch. 623 (SB 931, Renewable Energy Certainty Act, eff. 2025-07-01; HB 1036 is ch. 624). 2026 bills to change it (HB 460 lowering the priority preservation cap to 2 percent, SB 683, SB 265) show no action after committee hearings on mgaleg.maryland.gov as of 2026-10-09.

summary: State rule limits sound from routine operation of grid-scale and small-scale wind developments to 55 dBA by day and 42 dBA at night at protected locations, and 75 dBA at the project property line.
amendments_note: Rule amendment dates not shown on the copy read; not checked against the Secretary of State rule text.

summary: No state agency or municipality may license, permit, lease or grant rights for an offshore wind turbine in state-owned submerged lands or territorial waters, except small short-term research turbines, the designated research array project, and port facilities or cables serving wind projects in federal waters.
amendments_note: Enacted by PL 2021, c. 407 (emergency, signed 2021-07-06); amended by PL 2025, c. 597, Pt. A, s33 (rename of the former Governor's Energy Office; no change to the prohibition). As shown on legislature.maine.gov 2026-10-09.

summary: A solar development approved under the Site Location of Development Act on high-value agricultural land must pay a compensation fee based on the affected area (reducible for dual-use agrivoltaics) or permanently conserve an equal area of farmland.
amendments_note: Enacted by PL 2023, c. 448; amended by PL 2025, c. 597, Pt. A, s59 (agency renaming). As shown on legislature.maine.gov 2026-10-09.

summary: Developers of solar of 50 MW or more, wind of 100 MW or more, or storage of 50 MW and 200 MWh or more may seek a siting certificate from the Public Service Commission, and a local unit may ask the commission to require one; if the local unit has a compatible renewable energy ordinance the developer must apply locally first, and smaller projects stay under local zoning.
amendments_note: Sections added by 2023 PA 233, effective Nov. 29, 2024 (after the inventory was written, as the inventory notes). No amendment shown in the section history on legislature.mi.gov as of 2026-10-09.

summary: When the commission issues a certificate, it preempts any local rule that prohibits, regulates or is more restrictive than the certificate, and zoning changes made after the application cannot limit the facility; local ordinances also may not bar site testing.
amendments_note: Added by 2023 PA 233, effective Nov. 29, 2024. No amendment shown in the section history on legislature.mi.gov as of 2026-10-09.

summary: Certificated facilities must meet statutory standards: solar and storage 300 ft from nonparticipating dwellings and 50 ft from property lines and roads, solar panels no taller than 25 ft, wind turbines 2.1 times tip height from nonparticipating residences, 30 hours a year shadow flicker, and 55 dBA at nonparticipating dwellings. A local ordinance stricter than these standards is not "compatible".
amendments_note: Added by 2023 PA 233, effective Nov. 29, 2024. No amendment shown in the section history on legislature.mi.gov as of 2026-10-09.

summary: A large electric power generating plant may not be sited where its developed portion uses more than 0.5 acres of prime farmland per MW unless there is no feasible and prudent alternative; the rule does not apply inside or near cities.
amendments_note: Rule history 27 SR 1295; L 2005 c 97 art 3 s 19. Not among the chapter 7850 parts repealed by 2024 Minn. Laws c. 126 art. 7 s. 15 (that list skips 7850.4000 to 7850.4400 except 4100 and 4200). No later change shown on revisor.mn.gov as of 2026-10-09.

summary: The Major Facility Siting Act does not cover wind, solar or storage (its generation definition is limited to coal, oil, gas and hydro), so siting is left to county zoning.
amendments_note: 75-20-104 last amended 2021 (Ch. 13, 291, 409, L. 2021) per the 2025 MCA history note. 2025 Mont. Laws Ch. 761 added a statewide wind setback (see MT-state_setback_standard-1). 2025 HB 31 amended the wind and solar decommissioning bond law (75-26-304, 75-26-308), which is not a siting rule. Checked MCA 2025 on leg.mt.gov, 2026-10-09.

summary: After January 1, 2026, a wind turbine built under a wind energy agreement that is 500 ft or taller to blade tip may not be placed within 1,500 ft of an occupied residence unless the property owner approves a shorter distance; such turbines near homes in icing areas must also mitigate ice throw.
statute_citation: Mont. Code Ann. sections 75-26-402, 75-26-403 (2025 Mont. Laws Ch. 761)
amendments_note: New after the inventory: enacted by 2025 Mont. Laws Ch. 761, sections 1 and 2; applies after January 1, 2026. No later amendment in MCA 2025 history as of 2026-10-09.
source: Mont. Code Ann. sections 75-26-402, 75-26-403 (2025 Mont. Laws Ch. 761)

summary: Wind plants over 0.5 MW, other generation over 50 MW and utility-scale storage of 5 MW or more need a PSC certificate of site compatibility, and the certificate cannot override local zoning, so both the state and local zoning must approve.
amendments_note: Storage added by 2023 HB 1097 (eff. 2023-04-12, per the Legislative Council 2023 title summary); definitions renumbered by 2025 HB 1539 (enrolled bill seen as a search snippet). Chapter PDF on ndlegis.gov created 2025-07-02; 2026 special sessions not checked.

summary: Sites for PSC-certified wind facilities must exclude land within 1.1 times turbine height of a nonparticipating owner's property line and within 3 times turbine height of a nonparticipating owner's inhabited rural residence, unless all parties agree to a variance; local zoning may require more.
amendments_note: Section history not shown in the chapter PDF (created 2025-07-02); no 2025 change to 49-22-05.1 found. Not checked for 2026 special sessions.

summary: Privately developed wind and solar facilities are exempt from Power Review Board approval once the owner files certifications (including local decommissioning compliance and, above 10 MW, a public meeting), leaving siting to county and city zoning; the board must still approve generation built by public power suppliers and private energy storage.
amendments_note: 70-1014.02 amended by Laws 2024, LB399 and LB1370; Laws 2025, LB43 (military installation notice) and LB521. 70-1012 amended by Laws 2024, LB1370 (private energy storage approval), Laws 2025, LB43 and Laws 2026, LB1010 (effective July 18, 2026). Per source notes on nebraskalegislature.gov as of 2026-10-09.

summary: The Site Evaluation Committee must certify renewable facilities over 30 MW and storage of 30 MW or more, and may take jurisdiction over renewable facilities of 5 to 30 MW; smaller projects are under local zoning.
statute_citation: N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. 162-H:2, VII and XII
amendments_note: Source note on gc.nh.gov ends with 2024, 212:2, eff. July 19, 2024 and 2024, 295:1, eff. July 26, 2024 (after the inventory); 162-H:2, VII(g) now includes electrical storage of 30 MW or more. No 2025 or 2026 amendment shown as of 2026-10-09.
source: N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. 162-H:2, VII and XII

summary: New Jersey has no state siting permit for onshore solar or wind; municipalities decide under the Municipal Land Use Law, subject to state rules that make these facilities a permitted use on certain sites and to state environmental permits.
amendments_note: P.L.2026, c.84 (S3183, approved Sept. 9, 2026, effective immediately) amended 40:55D-66.11 and 66.16; see NJ-local_preemption-1.

summary: Solar, wind and battery storage facilities on 10 or more contiguous acres under one owner are a permitted use in every industrial or commercial district, and solar and storage on rooftops, landfills, brownfields, contaminated sites, mining sites and closed extraction sites (wind on landfills and closed extraction sites outside the Pinelands) are a permitted use in every municipality.
amendments_note: Amended by P.L.2026, c.84 (S3183), approved Sept. 9, 2026 per the legislature bill history API: 66.11 acreage cut from 20 to 10 acres, commercial districts and storage added; 66.16 adds battery storage and rooftop, brownfield, contaminated and mining sites. Effective immediately.

summary: In the Pinelands Preservation Area, Special Agricultural Production Area and Forest Areas, solar facilities as a principal use are allowed only on closed landfills, remediated contaminated sites or previously mined land, on previously disturbed portions, with Pinelands Development Credit purchases in many cases.
amendments_note: New rule R.2012 d.012, effective 1/3/2012 (43 N.J.R. 928(a), 44 N.J.R. 72(a)); no later amendment shown on law.cornell.edu as of 2026-10-09.

summary: A generating plant of 300 MW or more built for sale to the public needs location approval from the Public Regulation Commission; smaller plants are left to county and municipal zoning.
amendments_note: Could not check the official history note (nmonesource.com returned HTTP 403). Search-index text of the 2025 edition of the code shows the same 300,000 kW threshold. No 2024-2026 bill amending 62-9-3 found in a search of nmlegis.gov results; not confirmed.

summary: For plants that need Commission location approval, the Commission may declare a state, county or municipal land use regulation void as to the siting if it finds the regulation unreasonably restrictive and compliance not in the public interest; its judgment is conclusive on siting and local requirements.
amendments_note: Official history note not readable (HTTP 403). The 2025 edition text seen in search snippets matches; no 2024-2026 amendment found, not confirmed.

summary: Renewable generating plants over 70 MW need a utility facility permit from the Public Utilities Commission, which may issue only if the location conforms to local law and the applicant has or is seeking local approvals; plants of 70 MW or less need only local and other approvals.
amendments_note: 704.860 last amended 2019; 704.865 last amended 2007; 704.890 last amended 2019, per section history in NRS chapter 704 (revised 4/15/2026, 2025 session) on leg.state.nv.us. None after the inventory found.

summary: Local governments may not adopt rules that prohibit or unreasonably restrict a property owner from using a solar or wind energy system on the owner property, though reasonable wind rules on location, noise, safety and setback, and denials for safety or incompatibility, remain allowed.
amendments_note: 278.02077 last amended 2017; 278.0208 last amended 2009, per NRS chapter 278 (revised 9/9/2026, 2026R1) on leg.state.nv.us. None after the inventory.

state_body: Office of Renewable Energy Siting and Electric Transmission (ORES), Department of Public Service
summary: For facilities under ORES review, ORES may decline to apply a local law found unreasonably burdensome in view of the state's climate targets, and once a municipality has notice of the application it may not require its own approval, permit or other condition except as Article VIII allows.
amendments_note: Replaces former N.Y. Executive Law § 94-c(5)(e) cited by the inventory; Article VIII last revised 2024-06-21 per nysenate.gov. Later amendments not checked.

summary: The Power Siting Board certificates generating plants of 50 MW or more and wind farms of 5 to 50 MW; county and township zoning governs smaller solar and wind, and counties hold a separate veto under SB 52 (see OH-local_opt_out-1).
amendments_note: 4906.01 and 4906.10 amended by 2025 Ohio HB 15 (136th GA), eff. 2025-08-14: 4906.10(D) now requires a Board decision within 150 days after an application is complete or it is deemed approved; HB 15 also added advanced transmission technology language. 303.213 and 519.213 last amended by HB 501 (134th GA), eff. 2023-04-06. 4906.13 last amended 2019 (HB 6); 4906.20 last amended 2014 (HB 483).

summary: No political subdivision may require any approval, permit or other condition for a major utility facility or economically significant wind farm holding a Board certificate, apart from local rules unrelated to location, design or pollution control.
amendments_note: Last amended by HB 6 (133rd GA), eff. 2019-10-22; no later version on codes.ohio.gov as of 2026-10-09. Counties' SB 52 powers act before certification (see OH-local_opt_out-1).

summary: Turbines in Board-certificated wind farms must be at least 1.1 times total height from the wind farm property line and at least 1,125 feet from the blade tip to the nearest adjacent property line, unless all adjacent owners waive it.
amendments_note: Both sections last amended by 2014 Ohio HB 483 (130th GA), eff. 2014-09-15; no later version on codes.ohio.gov as of 2026-10-09.

summary: A board of county commissioners may designate all or part of the county's unincorporated area as a restricted area that bars large solar facilities and wind farms of 5 MW or more, and the Power Siting Board may not accept applications there; the county may also prohibit or shrink an individual project within 90 days after the developer's required public meeting.
amendments_note: 303.58 amended by 2024 Ohio HB 497 (135th GA), eff. 2025-04-09, adding newspaper, state public notice website or county website and social media as notice methods. 303.57, 303.59 to 303.62, 4906.021 and 4906.022 show only the SB 52 enactment (eff. 2021-10-11) in their version history on codes.ohio.gov as of 2026-10-09.

summary: Oklahoma has no state siting permit for wind or solar; the Corporation Commission takes notices and reports and enforces statutory wind setbacks, while any land use approval comes from county or municipal zoning where it exists.
statute_citation: Okla. Stat. tit. 17, §§ 160.11-160.23 (Oklahoma Wind Energy Development Act)
amendments_note: 160.21 has a 2023 version (SB 782, Laws 2023, c. 126, § 22). 2025-2026 wind setback bills HB 2751 (failed in Senate Energy committee) and SB 2 (failed on House reading) were not enacted per oklegislature.gov bill pages checked 2026-10-09. Title 17 PDF compiled 2025-12-31.
source: Okla. Stat. tit. 17, §§ 160.11-160.23 (Oklahoma Wind Energy Development Act)

summary: No wind energy facility tower may be built within 1.5 nautical miles of a public-use or municipal airport runway centerline, a public school or a hospital; separately, each turbine needing an FAA Form 7460-1 needs an FAA no-hazard determination and Defense Department clearance before construction.
amendments_note: History note: added Laws 2015, c. 92; amended Laws 2017, c. 45; Laws 2018, c. 4; Laws 2019, c. 310 (HB 2118, emerg. eff. 2019-05-07); Laws 2023, c. 126, § 21 (eff. 2023-11-01). No 2025-2026 change (HB 2751 and SB 2 not enacted).

summary: The Energy Facility Siting Council certificates wind plants of 100 MW average capacity or more (300 MW peak under the 3.00 wind factor), solar thermal plants of 25 MW or more, and solar PV using more than 240, 2,560 or 3,840 acres depending on land class; counties handle smaller projects unless the developer or county elects state review.
amendments_note: The inventory's thresholds are out of date. 469.300 history: 2023 c.336; 2024 c.25 (HB 4015, battery storage); 2025 c.162 (HB 3874) raised the wind threshold from 50 to 100 MW average. Solar PV acreage is now 240/2,560/3,840 (inventory: 160/1,280/1,920). 2026 Or. Laws c.12 (HB 4031, eff. 91 days after 2026 sine die) amends 469.320 to exempt solar, wind, geothermal and marine facilities from the site certificate if local land use approval is applied for by 2028-12-31 and the project meets federal tax credit begin-construction and in-service conditions.

summary: A Council site certificate binds all counties and cities as to site approval, and they must then issue the permits it addresses without further hearings; the Council may also find land use compliance despite unmet local criteria by taking a goal exception.
amendments_note: 469.401 history ends with 2025 c.305. 469.504 amended by 2026 Or. Laws c.46 (HB 4076), which adds a goal-exception finding for facilities using an existing plant's surplus interconnection.

summary: State land use rules cap solar PV on farmland that counties approve without a goal exception at 12 acres of high-value farmland, 20 acres of arable land and 320 acres of nonarable land, with a larger alternative path in eastern Oregon.
amendments_note: Rule history on the Secretary of State site: LCDD 5-2019 (eff. 2019-05-30, the rule Sabin describes), then LCDD 4-2021, LCDD 14-2024 (eff. 2025-01-01), LCDD 6-2025 (eff. 2026-01-01) and LCDD 10-2026 (eff. 2026-10-01). Section (44) lets eastern Oregon counties allow up to 160 acres on qualifying high-value farmland, 1,280 acres on arable land and 1,920 acres on non-arable land.

summary: Pennsylvania has no state siting permit for wind or solar; municipalities (and counties where a municipality has no zoning) regulate them through zoning under the Municipalities Planning Code.
statute_citation: Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code, Act of July 31, 1968, P.L. 805, No. 247, §§ 601, 602, 619 (53 P.S. §§ 10601, 10602, 10619)
amendments_note: The current compiled MPC on palegis.us shows a 2024 amendment (Act 44 of 2024, electronic transmittal, section 110) unrelated to energy siting; no 2024-2026 state wind or solar siting law found.
source: Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code, Act of July 31, 1968, P.L. 805, No. 247, §§ 601, 602, 619 (53 P.S. §§ 10601, 10602, 10619)

summary: Generating facilities of 40 MW or more are major energy facilities licensed by the Energy Facility Siting Board; smaller facilities are regulated by city and town zoning.
amendments_note: None since the inventory: history notes on webserver.rilegislature.gov end with P.L. 2001, ch. 145 (42-98-3) and P.L. 1994, ch. 14 (42-98-7), as of 2026-10-09.

summary: For major energy facilities the Siting Board is the licensing authority for every permit or variance that state law or local ordinance would require; local boards hear the matter but only send findings and a recommendation to the Siting Board.
amendments_note: History ends with P.L. 1994, ch. 14; none shown as of 2026-10-09.

summary: Any electric generating plant able to run at more than 75 MW is a major utility facility that needs a certificate of environmental compatibility and public convenience and necessity from the Public Service Commission before construction; smaller plants are left to county and municipal land use control.
amendments_note: Section histories on scstatehouse.gov (read 2026-10-09): 58-33-20 amended by 2025 Act No. 41 (H.3309, South Carolina Energy Security Act), sec. 19.A, eff 2025-05-12, adding (10) "like facility" (replacement at an existing generation site, up to 300 MW non-nuclear); (2)(a) reenacted with no change, so the 75 MW threshold stands. 58-33-110 rewritten by the same Act, sec. 20: replacement of an existing facility with a like facility is no longer construction of a major utility facility. 58-33-160 also amended by Act 41 (wording of (1)); (1)(e) unchanged in substance.

summary: When certifying a major utility facility (over 75 MW), the Public Service Commission may refuse to apply a local law or regulation it finds unreasonably restrictive as applied to the facility, and must state its reasons in its order.
amendments_note: 58-33-160 amended by 2025 Act No. 41, sec. 20, eff 2025-05-12 (the commission "must" grant a certificate if the applicant makes the listed showings; (1)(d) adds consideration of alternatives); the local-law override in (1)(e) reads the same. No later history shown on scstatehouse.gov as of 2026-10-09.

state_body: South Carolina Department of Environmental Services (enforcement)
summary: In a county with neither rural zoning nor a solar ordinance, a solar energy system with a footprint over 13 acres must meet state default standards: 50 ft setback from property lines and road rights of way, 200 ft from the nearest residence, church or school, 15 ft maximum height, a vegetative buffer, fencing and a decommissioning plan, after a county public hearing; the Department of Environmental Services enforces with civil penalties.
amendments_note: New section added by 2025 Act No. 41 (H.3309), sec. 8.A, eff 2025-05-12; per sec. 8.B it applies to projects approved by a county on or after 2026-01-01. Postdates the June 2024 inventory. No later amendment shown on scstatehouse.gov as of 2026-10-09.

summary: Wind and solar facilities of 100 MW or more (and expansions of 25 MW or more that bring a facility to 100 MW) need a Public Utilities Commission permit; the Commission does not choose or mandate locations, and county and municipal zoning still applies, while smaller projects are left to local governments alone.
amendments_note: Section histories on sdlegislature.gov (read 2026-10-09): 49-41B-2 amended by SL 2025, ch 193, sec. 1 (adds "hybrid facility" and folds hybrids of 100 MW or more into "energy conversion facility"); the 100 MW wind and solar definitions read as in the inventory. Chapter amended by SL 2026, ch 187 (local review committee and notice procedures for energy conversion facilities, 49-41B-5 to -14), not affecting the wind and solar thresholds. SL 2024, ch 189 amendments (carbon pipeline bill) were rejected by referendum on 2024-11-05.

summary: Each tower of a large wind energy system (tower 75 feet or taller) must be set back at least 500 feet or 1.1 times tower height, whichever is greater, from any surrounding property line, unless the adjacent landowner agrees in writing to a closer placement.
amendments_note: Source line on sdlegislature.gov shows only SL 2009, ch 221, sec. 4; no amendment as of 2026-10-09. A web search found no 2025 or 2026 South Dakota wind setback act.

summary: The Public Utility Commission may not issue a certificate for a wind facility with any turbine taller than 350 feet sited on a mountain ridge above 2,500 feet elevation or 500 feet or more above the adjacent valley floor (single on-site turbines under 100 feet are exempt).
statute_citation: Tenn. Code Ann. § 65-4-201 (subsection added by 2018 Tenn. Pub. Acts ch. 825, sec. 16)
amendments_note: No later amendment found, not confirmed against the codified history note. 2025 HB 149 / SB 132 (would extend the chapter to solar facilities of 5 MW or more) was last acted on 2025-01-28 (referred to subcommittee) per wapp.capitol.tn.gov, and 2025 SB 598 stalled after second consideration on 2025-02-12; neither was enacted as far as the bill pages show on 2026-10-09.
source: Tenn. Code Ann. § 65-4-201 (subsection added by 2018 Tenn. Pub. Acts ch. 825, sec. 16)

summary: Texas has no state siting permit for wind, solar or storage plants; municipalities regulate land use through zoning, and counties have no general zoning power, so projects in unincorporated areas face little local land use review.
amendments_note: 211.003 history: last amended 2003 (Acts 2003, 78th Leg., ch. 731). 2025 SB 819 (89th Leg., R.S.), which would have required a state permit for wind and solar of 10 MW or more with statewide setbacks, passed the Senate and was last acted on 2025-04-22 (referred to House State Affairs) per capitol.texas.gov; not enacted. No other 2025 or 2026 siting act found.

summary: For a permit by rule, a project that would disturb more than 10 acres of prime agricultural soils or 50 acres of contiguous forest (or any enrolled forestry preservation land) is deemed to have a significant adverse impact and must submit a mitigation plan with a 45-day public comment period.
amendments_note: Added by 2022 c. 688 per the section history; no later amendment shown as of 2026-10-09. 9VAC15-60-20(D) exempts projects with an interconnection request accepted by 2024-12-31.

summary: No company or person may begin site preparation or construction of an in-state electric generation or energy storage facility (other than one used solely for the owner's on-site consumption) without a certificate of public good from the Public Utility Commission, which must give due consideration to municipal and regional recommendations.
amendments_note: History note on legislature.vermont.gov ends with 2025, No. 38, secs. 3, 4, eff. 2025-07-01 (S.50; per a news summary it changed the 248(s) mid-size solar tier to over 25 kW); the site says it includes the actions of the 2025 session. Earlier changes since the inventory: 2023, No. 142 (Adj. Sess.), sec. 6, eff. 2024-05-30. 2026 session acts were not confirmed; a search found 2026 H.710 (plant definition) but no enacted 2026 change to section 248.

summary: Municipal zoning bylaws may not regulate generation, storage or transmission facilities reviewed under section 248; towns keep only solar screening rules (which the Commission applies unless they would effectively prohibit the facility) and substantial deference to energy-compliant town and regional plans.
amendments_note: 4413 history: last amended 2023, No. 181 (Adj. Sess.), sec. 53, eff. 2024-06-17, and 2023, No. 121 (Adj. Sess.), sec. 8a, eff. 2028-01-01; neither changes subsection (b) as far as the current text shows. 248: History note on legislature.vermont.gov ends with 2025, No. 38, secs. 3, 4, eff. 2025-07-01 (S.50; per a news summary it changed the 248(s) mid-size solar tier to over 25 kW); the site says it includes the actions of the 2025 session. Earlier changes since the inventory: 2023, No. 142 (Adj. Sess.), sec. 6, eff. 2024-05-30. 2026 session acts were not confirmed; a search found 2026 H.710 (plant definition) but no enacted 2026 change to section 248.

summary: Ground-mounted solar facilities approved under section 248 must be set back at least 100 feet from state or town highways and 50 feet from other property lines when larger than 150 kW (smaller tiers for smaller plants); the Commission may require more, or accept less by agreement with the town and adjoining owners.
amendments_note: History note on legislature.vermont.gov ends with 2025, No. 38, secs. 3, 4, eff. 2025-07-01 (S.50; per a news summary it changed the 248(s) mid-size solar tier to over 25 kW); the site says it includes the actions of the 2025 session. Earlier changes since the inventory: 2023, No. 142 (Adj. Sess.), sec. 6, eff. 2024-05-30. 2026 session acts were not confirmed; a search found 2026 H.710 (plant definition) but no enacted 2026 change to section 248.

state_body: Energy Facility Site Evaluation Council (EFSEC), with final decision by the Governor
summary: Wind, solar and storage projects are permitted by counties and cities unless the developer opts in to state certification; an applicant who opts in goes to the Energy Facility Site Evaluation Council, which recommends approval or rejection to the Governor, whose decision is final.
amendments_note: 80.50.060 history on app.leg.wa.gov (read 2026-10-09): 2026 c 244 s 1 and 2025 c 261 s 3 since the inventory (the current text also lists fusion energy facilities and adds tribal cultural resource notice; the opt-in for alternative energy resource and storage facilities reads as before). 80.50.020 amended 2025 c 261 s 2. 80.50.100 last amended 2022 c 183. Content of 2026 c 244 not read.

state_body: Energy Facility Site Evaluation Council (EFSEC), with final decision by the Governor
summary: For projects that opt in to state certification, the state preempts regulation of location, construction and operating conditions; the Council holds a hearing on consistency with local plans and zoning and may recommend preempting inconsistent local rules, with conditions reflecting the purpose of the preempted rules.
amendments_note: 80.50.110 history: 1975-76 2nd ex.s. c 108 s 37 (no later amendment). 80.50.090 last amended 2022 c 183 s 9. As shown on app.leg.wa.gov 2026-10-09.

summary: A wind or solar plant of 100 MW or more (a large electric generating facility) needs a certificate of public convenience and necessity from the Public Service Commission; smaller plants not built by a public utility are permitted by cities, villages, towns and counties within state limits on local restrictions.
amendments_note: History note for 196.491 in the chapter PDF ends with 2021 a. 24, 239: no 2023-2025 act amended it, per the code published 2026-10-01 (through 2025 Wis. Act 247). 66.0401 history ends with 2009 a. 40.

summary: If a local ordinance would preclude or inhibit a facility that has received a Commission certificate of public convenience and necessity, the facility may proceed anyway.
amendments_note: No amendment to 196.491 after 2021 shown in the history note (code published 2026-10-01).

summary: No city, village, town or county may restrict a solar or wind energy system unless the restriction protects public health or safety, does not significantly raise cost or cut efficiency, or allows a comparable alternative; local wind rules may not be stricter than the Commission's wind siting rules.
amendments_note: History: 1981 c. 354; ...; 2009 a. 40 (last amendment), as shown on docs.legis.wisconsin.gov 2026-10-09.

summary: Commission rules set the wind siting standards that local ordinances may not exceed and that the Commission applies to its own reviews: turbine setbacks of the lesser of 1,250 feet or 3.1 times blade tip height from non-participating residences and occupied community buildings, 1.1 times tip height from non-participating property lines and roads, and noise limits of 50 dBA by day and 45 dBA at night.
amendments_note: Chapter PSC 128 as published in Register November 2024 No. 827 (read 2026-10-09); 128.02 and 128.03 history shows creation by CR 10-057, eff. 2011-03-01. Whether any section changed in the 2024 republication was not checked.

summary: Every wind or solar facility over 0.5 MW needs a permit from the board of county commissioners; in addition, wind facilities of 20 or more turbines and solar facilities over 30 MW or disturbing 100 acres or more need an Industrial Siting Council permit, and a county may refer a smaller project to the Council.
amendments_note: Compiled text dated 2026-05-08 read; no history notes in the compilation. 2025 SF 183 (a moratorium on new wind and solar projects) died in committee per news reports; no enacted 2024-2026 change to these sections found in a web search, not confirmed on wyoleg.gov bill pages.

summary: Counties may not permit a wind turbine closer than 110 percent of tower height to adjoining property lines and public roads, 5.5 times tower height (at least 1,000 feet) to a dwelling or platted subdivision, or half a mile to a city or town limit, or within two nautical miles of an active military missile launch or control facility without military and FAA clearances; solar arrays must stay 300 feet from occupied structures, 100 feet inside the facility boundary and 100 to 200 feet from roads, though counties may vary the solar setbacks. County rules may not be less stringent for wind.
amendments_note: Compiled text dated 2026-05-08 read; no history notes in the compilation. 2025 SF 183 (a moratorium on new wind and solar projects) died in committee per news reports; no enacted 2024-2026 change to these sections found in a web search, not confirmed on wyoleg.gov bill pages.
